extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and parties involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED staff, ALJs, accused practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, procedures, and evaluative criteria governing disciplinary proceedings for practitioners before the USPTO, including required practitioner duties (communication, diligence), procedural consequences (default, service), burden of proof, and factors for deciding sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to discipline practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and to discipline a practitioner under 35 U.S.C. § 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory authority is the basis for USPTO regulations and disciplinary actions; any disciplinary action must afford notice and opportunity for hearing as required by 35 U.S.C. § 32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity for hearing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must receive notice and an opportunity for a hearing before disciplinary action is taken (statutory requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings must provide the accused an opportunity to answer and be heard; failure to provide adequate notice could undermine the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures governing disciplinary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary hearings are conducted in accordance with 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C, and with section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by a hearing officer appointed by the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 C.F.R. part 11 rules for service, filing, motions, evidentiary matters, and hearing conduct; practitioners should be aware that ALJs from HUD have been appointed to hear USPTO disciplinary cases per interagency agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Likewise, it is the respondent’s burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is a level between preponderance and beyond reasonable doubt; evidence must be certain, unambiguous, and persuasive enough to produce a firm belief or conviction in the trier of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to timely answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If respondent does not file an answer as required, the allegations may be taken as admitted and default may be entered; parties should timely respond or seek extensions per the procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service rules including service by publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If personal service cannot be effected, notice may be served via publication pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b); publication starts the clock for the respondent’s time to answer (30 days from second publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure service attempts comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a) and (b) (including service to the address on file under 11.11); understand timelines triggered by publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep contact/address information current
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep their contact information (address) current with the OED as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.11; failure to do so may be an independent violation and can affect service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining an accurate address is required so the Office can effect service; failing to update address may lead to additional sanctions or adverse procedural consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner oath/affirmation to observe USPTO rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners granted recognition to practice must sign an oath or affirmation that they will observe the laws and rules of practice of the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath creates an enforceable obligation to follow USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct; violations of the Rules can constitute breaches of that oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to Office actions, to take reasonable steps to revive applications, or otherwise abandoning client matters can violate this duty and support disciplinary charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not informing clients of Office actions, notices of abandonment, maintenance reminders, or patent expirations is a breach of this duty; clients must be told options and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to promptly comply with reasonable client information requests
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignoring client emails or inquiries and failing to provide substantive responses risks a disciplinary violation for lack of communication and abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to explain matters to permit informed client decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must explain Office actions, response options, potential consequences, and available remedial actions; cursory or misleading explanations can constitute misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing knowledge of adverse events (e.g., telling a client you'll investigate while having no intention to do so) is cited as an example of dishonesty warranting discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner’s fitness to practice before the Office. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent neglect, lack of candor, or failure to participate in proceedings can be treated as conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on violating or attempting to violate USPTO Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to violate or attempt to violate the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged violations of multiple ethics rules (communication, diligence, honesty) can be charged together under this overarching prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-address responsibilities (maintenance fee notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fee address of record (37 C.F.R. § 1.363) is used for maintenance fee notices; retaining that address and failing to notify the client or pay maintenance fees can result in patent expiration and disciplinary liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who accept maintenance-fee responsibilities must inform clients of reminders and options and must not allow patents to expire without client knowledge and consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction-determination factors
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations require the Court consider the following four factors in determining an appropriate sanction: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner’s conduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors frame the evaluation of an appropriate sanction (e.g., suspension, exclusion); the decisionmaker weighs duty violated, mental state, injury, and aggravating/mitigating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of legal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice from lawyers who have not discharged, will not discharge, or are unlikely to discharge their professional duties — not punishment per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions focus on protection of clients and the legal system; this principle guides selection and severity of sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards § 9.22 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors that warrant more severe sanction include: dishonest or selfish motive; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to participate or comply with orders; and substantial experience in the practice of law. (Citing ABA STANDARDS § 9.22.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present (especially dishonest motive or bad-faith obstruction), these factors support harsher discipline such as exclusion; other aggravating factors in the ABA Standards may also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (general consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of any mitigating factors should be considered when determining sanctions (as part of the fourth factor in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not exhaustively listed on this page, mitigating factors per ABA Standards (e.g., absence of prior discipline, remorse, restitution) may reduce sanction severity if shown by clear and convincing evidence.
